Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Determine how the Anti-Kickback Statute and Stark Law affect the referral patterns of
orthopaedic surgeons.
Assess how to use ancillary income opportunities available to orthopaedic surgeons.
Critically analyze the differences between hospital and private practice employment models.
Introduction
Ancillary income can be used to augment the revenue of physician groups.
The Anti-Kickback Statute and Stark Law are self-referral laws put in place more than 30 years
ago and are intended to protect against inappropriate referrals to physician-owned entities.


Introduction
Orthopaedic surgery reimbursement rates have steadily declined in the past 25 years,
whereas expenses and overhead costs have continued to increase. In the past, this gap
could be reduced by increasing volume alone; however, this is becoming increasingly
difficult to sustain.1
The ability to maintain a profitable practice depends on the revenue generated being
offset by applicable overhead costs. One of the methods physician groups can use to
augment their revenue is ancillary income. Ancillary income is revenue generated from
lines of business outside the core practice by physicians providing patient care and is a
method to reduce a practice’s overhead costs while providing more comprehensive and
efficient care. In addition to serving as an income source, physician-managed ancillary
care is more efficient and satisfying to patients than analogous care managed by large
healthcare organizations.2
Orthopaedic surgeons are one of the few subspecialties that are able to own and control
multiple ancillary services to which they can refer patients. Examples of these services
include physical therapy, MRI, durable medical equipment (DME), and electromyography
(EMG).
Self-referral laws were introduced more than 30 years ago at a time at which fee-for-
service reimbursement was in practice3, 4, 5 and are intended to provide guardrails to
protect against inappropriate referrals to physician-owned entities. The Anti-Kickback
Statute (AKS) was enacted in 1972 and prohibits anything of value to induce referrals for
any service paid by Medicare. The Stark Law was passed in 1992 and broadly prevents
physicians from referring patients for designated health services (DHS) if the physician or
an immediate family member has a financial relationship with the healthcare entity.4, 5
The legal issues affecting ancillary income are complicated and vary by state; therefore,
legal counsel familiar in this matter must be obtained.

Self-Referral Rules and Regulations and Certificate of Need
Anti-Kickback Statute
Enacted in 1972 as part of the Social Security Act amendments.
This statute makes it illegal for anyone to offer, solicit, make, or receive any payment that is
intended to induce referrals under a federal healthcare program.
Violation of this law is a felony; consequently, intent needs to be proven.

Anti-Kickback Statute
The AKS prohibits anything of value to induce referrals for services paid by any federal
healthcare program. These rules are regulated by the Office of Inspector General with
civil and criminal punishments for violation. Punishment for violation may include
imprisonment, fines, and exclusion from Medicare paying programs.4,6 Because the AKS
is criminal law, the intent of the physician to violate the statute must be proven. Safe
harbors that immunize certain payment and business practices exist to guide business
and provider relationships. To be protected by a safe harbor, all of its elements must be
satisfied. Some of the common safe harbors include protection for employee
compensation, practitioner recruitment to underserved areas, and sales of retiring
physicians’ practices to other physicians.7
Stark Law
Set of US federal laws passed more than 30 years ago that prohibit physician self-referral.
This law specifically relates to Medicare or Medicaid patients and their referral for DHS.
This law was intended to be clearer and less ambiguous than the AKS, so the intent of the
parties was made irrelevant.
Stark Law is civil; therefore, violation results in monetary penalties rather than imprisonment.
The most important exception under Stark Law covers in-office ancillary income. Physician
groups can provide almost all DHS services without penalty if they meet the exception
conditions. 
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:19 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002058


Stark Law
The Stark Law only applies to entities that provide DHS. Examples of these services are
clinical laboratory services, physical therapy, occupational therapy, radiology services,
DME and supplies, and outpatient prescription drugs. Multiple federal offices oversee
the enforcement of this law, including the Department of Justice, the Centers for
Medicare & Medicaid Services, and the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).
The physician referring the patient, or the physician’s immediate family member, cannot
have any financial relationship with the entity.3-5 Several exceptions to this law exist,
including physician services, in-office ancillary services, and rental of office space and
equipment. Penalties for Stark Law violations are numerous. They include the refund of
monies received by physicians and facilities for amounts collected, payment of civil fines
as high as $15,000 for each DHS service provided to a patient in violation of the law,
exclusion from Medicare and state Medicaid programs, and payment of civil penalties for
attempting to circumvent the law of as high as $100,000 for each scheme.4,5
For practicing orthopaedic physicians, the most important exception under Stark Law
covers in-office ancillary income. If a physician group meets the exception conditions,
then they can provide almost all DHS services. To meet the exception, the practice has to
be qualified as a group. Practices must be careful because Stark Law defines the term
group very narrowly. The definition states that 75% of the services provided by the group
practice must be billed by the same organization. If more than 25% of billed services
from the group are from another organization, then the group will not qualify for this
exemption under Stark Law.4 In addition, at least 75% of the group’s patient encounters
must be performed by individuals who are considered members of the group. Therefore,
independent contractors who are not considered members of the group cannot provide
25% or more of the services billed. If the group practice is in violation, then it is no longer
considered a group, and the in-office ancillary exception cannot be used.4
A compensation formula must be created to allocate the income generated by ancillary
services among the group members because Stark Law places restrictions on how the
pool of money is divided. Compensation cannot account for the volume or value of
referrals of DHS by a physician. Crediting any physician for ordering a DHS is improper.4
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:19 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002058
4/25

In January 2021, Health and Human Services issued two highly anticipated final rules that
were named the Final Rule. The goal of this rule is to modernize and clarify the AKS and
Stark Law. According to Health and Human Services, the Final Rule is designed to allow
physicians more flexibility to participate in value-based arrangements and ease the
compliance burden while maintaining safeguards to protect patients and federal
healthcare programs from abuse. The Final Rule also adds new safe harbors and
provides clarification and revisions to existing guidance. For example, the addition of a
cybersecurity technology and services safe harbor to the AKS allows for the donation of
technology and services to providers who are unable to obtain their own. Limited
remuneration to a physician is an example of a new exception to the Stark Law. With this
exception, remuneration of as much as $5,000 aggregated in a calendar year is
permitted if certain requirements are met.8 This brief overview of the Final Rule is not
exhaustive, and physicians must stay up-to-date on the most current laws because they
are continuously changing.
The complexity of and lack of clear information about the AKS and Stark Law create an
obstacle for healthcare providers. In addition to federal law, physicians also must
consider the wide variations in state laws and regulations. Physicians should obtain legal
advice from an attorney well versed in the healthcare field before beginning any new
endeavors or arrangements.
Certificate of Need
Certificate of need (CON) laws regulate establishment or expansion of healthcare facilities and
services in a given area.
CON laws are state-regulated, and wide state-to-state variations exist.

Certificate of Need
In states with a CON program, a state health planning agency must approve the plan to
expand or open a new healthcare facility.4 Currently, 35 states and Washington, DC,
have a CON program in place; however, wide variation exists in the manner in which
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:19 AM
AAOS | Ancillary Partnerships and Income
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002058
5/25

each program is run.9 The proposed goal of this program is to reduce healthcare costs
by avoiding price inflations from large healthcare facilities that are not filling their beds.
These large facilities have fixed costs. If enough demand for their services exists, then
these facilities may charge higher prices for the beds they fill. The goal of CON programs
is to control cost by restricting duplicate services and determining if the proposed new
services meet the needs of the community. However, the reduced competition that this
law creates may lead to decreased quality and increased prices.
Ancillary Income Opportunities
Ambulatory Surgery Center/Orthopaedic Specialty Hospital
Ambulatory surgery centers (ASCs) and in-office surgery centers are not considered a DHS;
therefore, ownership of these entities by physicians is not subject to Stark Law and safe
harbor regulations.
ASCs have been shown to improve patient care.
Procedures performed at an ASC generate revenue from the facility fee, which is paid to the
physician group rather than the hospital.
The group must perform a payor and market analysis if considering incorporating an ASC into
the practice.
Ownership of an orthopaedic specialty hospital is another option; however, care must be
taken in considering this investment opportunity because of ongoing regulatory scrutiny.

Ambulatory Surgery Center/Orthopaedic Specialty Hospital
The AKS and Stark Law do not apply to ASCs.3-6 Many different models of ASC ownership
exist. The group can either build its own ASC or invest in an ASC through a joint venture
with a nonsurgical physician practice, a multispecialty physician practice, a health
maintenance organization, a hospital system, or an ASC specialty corporation.10 The
advantages of a joint venture arrangement include participating in a shared investment
and sharing its inherent financial risk, having an increased referral base, and creating the
possibility of increased efficiency and productivity. The disadvantages of a joint venture
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:19 AM
AAOS | Ancillary Partnerships and Income
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002058
6/25

arrangement include sharing the profits generated by the surgeons and differences in
management styles.10
A study performed by the Office of Inspector General showed that 98% of Medicare
patients were satisfied with their ASC experience and 91% preferred the ASC to the
hospital.6 These responses reflect that participating physicians have increased discretion
and oversight over staffing quantity and quality compared with physicians who practice
in large healthcare organizations. In large healthcare settings, clinical support staff
typically report directly to nonphysician managers. Studies also show that ASCs have a
faster turnover time compared with an inpatient setting. Mean hospital turnover time is
20 to 40 minutes, whereas in an ASC setting mean turnover time is 7 to 15 minutes or
even less, depending on the procedure.10 This is primarily because of an alignment of
incentives for the surgeons and staff of an ASC (in which the workday is done after all
cases have concluded) and a corresponding misalignment in large healthcare settings (in
which the workday is done for surgeons after cases are concluded, with support staff
working on an hourly basis). In addition to higher patient satisfaction and increased
efficiency, ASCs provide better surgical care for patients than large healthcare
organizations. The total operating room time is shorter, the infection rate is lower (0.15%
compared with 4% for the same procedure in a hospital), and the overall cost for
patients and payors is lower.6
Brent Lambert, MD, cofounder of Ambulatory Surgery Centers of America, said that
physicians augmenting their annual practice income by 15% to 20% through an ASC
investment is not uncommon.2 Ownership in an ASC may not only increase revenue for
physicians but also improve their overall satisfaction with their profession. If surgeries
are performed at an ASC, physicians have more control over the operations at the
facilities where they practice.
Ownership of an orthopaedic specialty hospital is another option for orthopaedic
surgeons. A specialty hospital allows surgeons to perform inpatient and outpatient
procedures and potentially receive higher payment rates; however, specialty hospitals
have many opponents, which makes investment in this model more risky. Under Stark
Law, physicians cannot invest in hospital departments; however, they can invest in the
entire hospital. Specialty hospitals use this exemption to allow physician ownership of
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:19 AM
AAOS | Ancillary Partnerships and Income
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002058
7/25

these hospitals. Ongoing regulatory scrutiny exists, which makes investment in a
specialty hospital considerably more risky than investment in an ASC.11
Physical Therapy and Occupational Therapy
Having physical therapy and occupational therapy services in the office is convenient for the
patient, provider, and physical therapist.
It Hiring and employing physical therapists rather than having an outside group rent space in
the office is more profitable.
In-office physical therapists have more access to the physician and are more comfortable with
specific providers’ protocols.

Physical Therapy and Occupational Therapy
Physical therapy and occupational therapy availability in a provider’s office increases
patients and providers satisfaction while increasing revenue for the physician. On-site
physical therapy is associated with many advantages. One advantage for the patient is
the convenience of scheduling physical therapy appointments directly after they receive
a referral. This convenience can translate into greater patient compliance because the
patient is already familiar and comfortable with the setting.12 Another advantage is the
ease of access the physical therapist has to patient medical records and possibly the
treating physician. Because of these on-site conveniences, the physical therapist will be
able to address patient needs in a timely fashion. Lastly, and possibly most importantly,
providers can hand-select and directly oversee the physical therapists, which can
improve overall outcomes and patient satisfaction.
The physician group must assess referral demand and payor mix before hiring physical
therapists. The most accurate method of predicting this demand is to track the current
external physical therapy referrals for a period. After the group determines the mean
number of referrals per physician, the next step is to determine the mean number of
visits per referral. These two variables allow for calculation of the total number of visits
per year so staffing needs can be predicted.12 The principal of Medical Practice
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:19 AM
AAOS | Ancillary Partnerships and Income
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002058
8/25

Consulting, John Davis, MBA, recommends practices employ their own physical
therapists and use the same tax identification number for the practice and the physical
therapy program to reduce the legal risk associated with referral law. Practices can
expect to generate $100,000 to $200,000 per year per provider, with a 25% to 30% profit
margin.2
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
The physician group can purchase an MRI machine and have MRIs read via teleradiology.
This can ensure high-quality radiologists are reading MRIs because they are hand-selected by
the physicians.
MRI technicians are hired by the group and are familiar with specific protocols and sequences,
which can ensure the correct MRIs are obtained.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
In-office MRI can dramatically increase efficiency in scheduling and augment income for
the physician group. MRI can be performed in the office, and the MRIs can be officially
read by a fellowship-trained musculoskeletal radiologist from a teleradiology
company.2,13 This example is the standard practice followed by many groups. Although
many orthopaedic physicians feel comfortable reading the MRIs they order, the current
standard of care is to have a radiologist perform the official interpretation. This
arrangement is the safest because payor concerns exist regarding who is qualified to
provide imaging.2,13 This model also can provide superior patient care because it can
ensure that the correct images and sequences are obtained and that a high-quality
radiologist is interpreting the images.
Purchasing an MRI machine requires a large up-front investment; therefore, a thorough
market analysis, referral analysis, and business plan must be performed before initiating
such a purchase. To determine whether purchasing an MRI machine is right for a group,
practices must project their volume based on past MRI referrals and determine the likely
payor mix because payments vary widely by payor. If purchasing an MRI machine, the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:19 AM
AAOS | Ancillary Partnerships and Income
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002058
9/25

cost of maintenance, appliance training, setup, and delivery must be considered because
it is important to keep the machine running efficiently.13
Ultrasonography
The physician group can purchase an ultrasonography machine for ultrasonographic-guided
injections.
Physicians can bill a Current Procedural Terminology code for ultrasonography-guided
injections to increase payout from these simple in-office procedures.
Ultrasonography-guided injections provide increased accuracy and increased patient
satisfaction.

Ultrasonography
Purchasing an ultrasonography machine is a low risk with the potential for high reward.
The cost of an ultrasonography machine can range from $15,000 to more than $75,000,
depending on the quality of the machine. Each time ultrasonography is used for an
injection, the portion of the payout related to its use goes into a collective pot that is
distributed evenly among the physician group members. Stark Law prohibits the group
from dividing the revenue based on the number of ultrasonographic-guided injections
the provider performs. The mean payout for ultrasonographic guidance for needle
placement, supervision, and interpretation is $150 to $200, in addition to the amount
that is already being collected for the injection. With the addition of an in-office
ultrasonography machine, a group has the ability to create additional profits, provide
superior accuracy, and increase patient satisfaction with overall care.
Electromyography
Many subspecialties in orthopaedics routinely order EMG.
In-office EMG is not only a convenience for the patient but also an opportunity to provide
superior overall care and generate ancillary revenue.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:19 AM
AAOS | Ancillary Partnerships and Income
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002058
10/25


Electromyography
EMG machines cost between $1,000 and $10,000. One model of offering in-office EMG
includes hiring a physiatrist to be part of the group. By having a physiatrist in the
practice, the group can collect the revenue from the referral rather than send the patient
outside the practice. The physiatrist can not only perform EMG but also administer pain
management injections and see nonsurgical orthopaedic patients. Another model for
the group practice is to contract a physiatrist hourly to perform EMG on-site. If the group
owns the facility, they can rent out office space in the building to a physiatrist to enhance
patient care;2 however, renting out unused space is illegal if the practice is not the
outright owner of the building.
Durable Medical Equipment
A DME division that is owned entirely by a physician group is the most profitable model;
however, it also is the most time-consuming and difficult model to execute.
Three different joint business models exist: inventory model, combination stock-and-bill/billing
for select items, and shared revenue.

Durable Medical Equipment
The main goal of the group should be to balance a periodic automatic replenishment
level that provides adequate DME for patients without purchasing excess stock that sits
unused on a shelf. A completely group-owned model and three joint business models
exist. The group should determine which model is the most profitable and the most
beneficial for their patients. The group can petition the major Medicare insurance
company in the area to assess their office and their ability to provide DME. After the
group gets credentialed, they can dispense anything that a federally insured patient can
get at a stand-alone, commercial, third-party DME supply company.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:19 AM
AAOS | Ancillary Partnerships and Income
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002058
11/25

The inventory-control scanner model offered by third-party vendors is one in which a
sophisticated mobile scanner is used to regulate the inventory tracking issues that most
groups face. The main advantage of this model is that the group is better able to
accurately monitor existing product levels, incorporate a reorder mechanism to ensure
replenishment while minimizing periodic automatic replenishment levels, and associate
dispensed items with accurate billing and patient charges. This model may be associated
with a license fee and monthly usage charges in addition to the cost of the scanners;
therefore, substantial drawbacks are associated with this design.14 The combination
stock-and-bill/billing for select items model is one in which a vendor allows the group to
independently bill for select items; however, the group also allows the vendor to
maintain a stock-and-bill format for the remaining items for which the group cannot
obtain reimbursement.14 Lastly, the shared-revenue model is one in which a vendor
supplies a worker to act as the designated staff member in charge of fitting and
inventory. The vendor then bills the item and deducts the cost of the provided worker’s
salary, billing fees and cost of goods sold. The leftover profit is then split among the
group and vendor based on a predetermined percentage.14 One of the main
disadvantages of this model is that the final profit of the group is a fraction of what it
would be if they had developed their own division.
Having an in-office DME division is extremely convenient for patients and offers the
physician group an opportunity for increased revenue. The group must carefully analyze
the referral base and create a sound business plan before initiating this service because
many factors can lead to an overall loss for the group. These factors include increased
cost of products, inability to capture all referrals, and the unknown of future
requirements. The requirements for precertification and which DME items are
reimbursable by each payor must be understood to generate profit from this service.
Advanced Practice Providers
The physician group can hire physician assistants and/or nurse practitioners to assist in the
office and in the operating room.
One model of employing advanced practice providers (APPs) is to treat their salaries as
overhead cost and divide the leftover revenue they generate among the physicians supervising
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:19 AM
AAOS | Ancillary Partnerships and Income
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002058
12/25

them.
Another model is to have physicians who want a physician assistant/nurse practitioner cover
the salary of the physician assistant/nurse practitioner from their own revenue; however, then
they alone are able to keep the excess income generated.

Advanced Practice Providers
APPs see their own patients and can perform injections. They are expected to cover their
salary and benefits through clinical activity and cost avoidance (eg, performing unbillable
clinical visits during the 90-day global period postoperatively, which frees up physicians
to engage in other revenue-generating activity). Another model of employing APPs is to
have the physicians who want physicians assistants or nurse practitioners cover their
salary from their own revenue, and they alone are able to keep any excess income for
themselves. APPs may increase the efficiency of the surgeon in the office and in the
operating room. This increase in efficiency may mean increased revenue for the surgeon
and the group because they are able to see more patients and perform more surgeries
in the same allotted amount of time.
Pharmacy
Physician offices can dispense prescription medications to patients covered by workers’
compensation, personal injury protection, and commercial preferred provider organization
insurance plans.
This in-office service offers patients convenience and improves their overall satisfaction while
increasing revenue for the group.

Pharmacy
Third-party programs are available to help physician groups setup and manage an in-
office pharmacy. Orthopaedic surgery offices commonly prescribe anti-inflammatory
agents, antibiotic agents, muscle relaxers, and medications to manage neuropathic pain.
An in-office pharmacy can dispense opioid medications; however, this should be done
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:19 AM
AAOS | Ancillary Partnerships and Income
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002058
13/25

with great caution. Regulations regarding the requirements to prescribe and dispense
medications in-office vary by state; therefore, physician groups must research and follow
the law as determined by the state. The prescriptions are delivered packaged with a
predetermined allocated number of pills. Vendors can provide a group with software
that dispenses medications in compliance with federal and state regulations, checks for
medication side effects, and accurately reports controlled substances. The medications
are purchased close to cost, allowing room to generate revenue. This in-office service is
more convenient for the patient and the provider.
Consulting and Product Development
Income from consulting must be based on expertise in a specific field without considering the
amount of product used or the physician’s status as a referring physician or the arrangement
will violate the AKS.
Physicians with product inventions can start their own business or sell their idea to an
established company.

Consulting and Product Development
Consulting for one of the many companies that provide orthopaedic implants or services
can augment a physician’s income. The payment given to the physician must be
consistent with the value of his or her expertise and cannot be based on product usage
or referrals or it would violate the AKS.4
Product development is another opportunity to generate income. If a physician invents
and develops a product while in private practice, the physician can start a company or
sell the idea to an established entity and collect royalties from sales. Physicians must
consider negotiating intellectual property in reviewing a contract for an employed
position because some contracts give the employer complete ownership of the
physician’s ideas.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:19 AM
AAOS | Ancillary Partnerships and Income
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002058
14/25

Real Estate
Physician groups that own their own office buildings or ASCs can generate revenue by renting
out unused space.
The real estate portfolio of the group also can include other types of buildings or offices that
are unrelated to health care.

Real Estate
Renting out unused space provides an opportunity for a group to generate income.
Lease of office space generally is permissible if certain conditions are met. The lease
must be in writing and signed by both parties, the space must be used exclusively by the
lessee, the space must be used for a legitimate purpose, the term of the lease must be at
least 1 year, and the rental charges must be set in advance.4 The rental charge must be
consistent with fair market value and exclusive to the volume or value of referrals
between the parties.4
Legal
Independent Medical Examination
Independent medical examinations (IMEs) are performed on behalf of insurance companies,
attorneys, case managers, and/or other entities that request they be performed.
The physician reviews a patient’s records, examines the patient, and provides a written report
on the findings.
Additional income can be generated from follow-up dispositions and trial testimony.

Independent Medical Examination
IME appointments require minimal overhead because they can be performed in rented
or subleased office space without staffing if necessary. Some physicians continue to
perform IMEs after they have stopped clinical practice because it is a good method to
generate income with little liability. More than 80 million referrals for IMEs are made
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:19 AM
AAOS | Ancillary Partnerships and Income
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002058
15/25

each year, which represents an estimated $180 billion.6 Highly sought-after physicians
who perform IMEs can earn hundreds of thousands of dollars per year.
Expert Witness
Physicians can charge a fee if requested to be an expert witness in court.
The fee includes an hourly charge for file review/preparation and an hourly fee for testimony.
Standards of professionalism apply to all Fellows and members of the American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons who serve as an expert witness. 

Expert Witness
Being an expert witness can augment income for a physician. Physicians must consider if
this revenue is advantageous because they likely will lose their normal daily earnings if
not performing surgeries or seeing patients in the office while they are in court
proceedings. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons has mandatory standards
of professionalism that were created to ensure no fraudulent expert witness testimony
occurs. Four standards must be followed by all Fellows and members of the American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons: impartial testimony, subject matter knowledge,
qualifications, and compensation (Resource 1). Physicians cannot knowingly provide an
expert opinion that is false and cannot provide an opinion on a subject matter that is
outside their expertise. Accepting compensation that is deemed excessive or based on
the outcome of the proceedings also is unethical. 
Hospital and Health System Leadership Roles
These paid leadership positions can increase a physician’s income and influence within the
hospital.

Hospital and Health System Leadership Roles
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:19 AM
AAOS | Ancillary Partnerships and Income
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002058
16/25

Physicians can hold many hospital and health system leadership roles. These positions
range from chief medical officer to department chair. Physicians can increase their
influence and augment their income by becoming involved in hospital leadership.
Physicians can hold one of these positions and still continue to practice if their role is
part-time. A physician must carefully consider agreeing to serve in hospital or health
system leadership because the role may limit the ability to buy into an ASC that is
partially owned by another healthcare entity.
Employment Models
51% of orthopaedic surgeons will change employers within the first 5 years of practice.
Practice type and location are commonly cited as the most important factors in searching for a
job.
Employment trends show increasing numbers of hospital-employed orthopaedic surgeons
compared with those in private practice.

Employment Models
Selecting the correct employment opportunity is a difficult decision, with many variables
to be considered. Location, compensation, practice type, research opportunities, and
other factors may play a role in overall surgeon satisfaction. Many residents complete
training with little to no guidance on how to successfully select from various options. A
study by Laratta et al15 found that among surveyed orthopaedic physicians, 51% left
their first job before finishing their fifth year of practice. Those who remained and those
who left their first job cited location and practice type as the most important factors in
their decisions.
According to the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons 2018 Census, 57% of
surveyed orthopaedic physicians stated they practice in some type of private practice
setting, 17% responded they were employed in a hospital/medical center, and 15% were
employed by an academic practice institution.16 This is in contrast to the American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons 2012 census, which showed that 71% of surveyed
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:19 AM
AAOS | Ancillary Partnerships and Income
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002058
17/25

orthopaedic physicians stated they practice in some type of private practice setting, 9%
responded they were employed in a hospital/medical center, and 9% were employed by
an academic practice institution.17 Other practice model responses included military
practice, public institutions, and locum tenens.16,17 The trend toward increasing
percentages of hospital-employed physicians has left many wondering if private practice
will remain a viable option in the future (Figures 1 and 2).

Hospitals can offer new surgeons a guaranteed/sustained income while building a practice.19
Hospital-employed physicians typically do not deal with payor or insurance contracts.18,20
Billing, reimbursements, and uninsured patient issues are handled by the hospital and not the
physician, allowing the physician to focus on patient care and avoid the burden of
administrative duties.20,21
Access to other services and specialties is more readily available if the physician is part of a
larger hospital system.22
The physician has a built-in and potentially more robust referral base if part of a larger
hospital system.22
Potential for career growth within departments and systems21
Disadvantages
Limited opportunities for ancillary income18,20,22
Employed physicians lack operational control and must adhere to the rules of larger hospital
systems (hours/services available).18,20
Employment may limit a physician’s autonomy to make staffing decisions, which may be a long
process involving human resource departments.18-20,22
Renewal contracts may lack original incentives and even include noncompete clauses, making
transitions to other employment opportunities difficult.18-20

Hospital Employment
Hospital employment may be an appealing option for orthopaedic surgeons who want
income stability and to outsource the daily stresses of administrative responsibilities.
However, the original incentives may not be guaranteed over the course of a physician’s
career, and with stability, the physician may be forfeiting autonomy in various aspects of
patient care and day-to-day life. In addition, ancillary income opportunities often are
more limited.

Advantages
Full autonomy to make decisions about patient care, staffing, and record keeping18,22

Ability to establish a culture and the pace of the practice without hospital management

More opportunities for ancillary income18,20
Shifting emphasis on outpatient orthopaedic surgery may make private practice physicians

administrators/systems.20
Disadvantages
Base salaries often are lower than those of employed physicians, at least initially.21
The surgeon/group is responsible for payroll, overhead, and other expenses; if not met, these
will directly affect the bottom-line take-home pay.19
Physicians often lack protection from fluctuations in yearly income.20

Private Practice
A private practice may be a good fit for orthopaedic surgeons who value autonomy and
are willing to be involved in the business aspects of running a practice on a regular basis,
including pursuing opportunities at generating ancillary income. However, if the
responsibility of overseeing finances and administrative responsibilities is not of interest,
other employment models may be a better fit.
Summary
Ancillary income provides a method to augment revenue and offset the current trend of
decreasing reimbursement. 
Laws with regard to in-office services and ancillary income are continually changing; therefore,
surgeons should obtain legal counsel before offering any new service.

Advantages and disadvantages exist to hospital and private practice models; therefore,

Summary
The cost of health care continues to increase while reimbursement rates have steadily
declined. The Medical Group Management Association reported that almost 45 cents of
each dollar of revenue are used to cover a group’s overhead expenses.11 Ancillary
income provides a method to close this gap and augment revenue generated by
healthcare providers. Between 2000 and 2016, reimbursement decreased across all
orthopaedic subspecialties except oncology by a mean of 29%. Work relative value units
increased by a mean of 10%, but the value of the relative value unit decreased across all
orthopaedic subspecialties by a mean of 39%.1 Ancillary income provides a form of
insulation from the inevitability of production variability of the individual and group and
from decreasing reimbursement rates. A practice with good ancillary income
opportunities also is better able to recruit and retain high-quality surgeons.
Physician-managed patient care generally is more efficient and is associated with better
patient satisfaction than large organization–managed patient care; therefore, increased
opportunities for in-office care are good for the patient and the provider. This lesson is
intended to briefly discuss the different types of ancillary income opportunities for
orthopaedic physicians and is not meant to be exhaustive or used as legal advice
regarding these topics. Laws regarding in-office services and ancillary income are
constantly changing and vary widely from state to state; therefore, legal counsel that is
well vested in this matter must be obtained before starting a new venture.
After graduation, residents are faced with the decision to join a private practice or
become hospital employed. Because advantages and disadvantages are associated with
both practice models, this decision is very personal. Being a well-informed applicant and
knowing which questions to ask before signing a contract will lead to increased job
satisfaction.
